root.claim: One deterministic multitape Turing machine multiplies $n$-bit integers exactly in $O(n(\lg n)^{1-\kappa})$ worst-case time with $\kappa=2^{-182}$, refuting the $n\log n$ optimality conjecture in this model.
root.method: Build two fast tape procedures (address interchange and simultaneous butterfly layers), run them inside synthetic transforms, reduce integer multiplication to such a convolution by resampling, chirps and a Chinese-remainder layout, then check precision and total up the time

motivation.text: Scanning $\Theta(n)$ stored bits at each of $\Theta(\log n)$ transform levels costs $\Theta(n\log n)$, so a power saving needs a faster way to move addresses and a faster way to do butterfly levels, both inside a multiplication reduction that still gives exact integers.

quote.quote: We therefore need savings in both movement and arithmetic.

root.salient: The saving is a power of the logarithm, $(\lg n)^{1-\kappa}$ with the tiny $\kappa=2^{-182}$, and it arises with the same pattern twice: each of the two fast procedures comes from a linear network whose total rank is just below the trivial bound.
